issues.legal_issue: A pre-suit notice given by the karta on behalf of a Hindu joint family remains effective for a suit brought by the divided coparceners after partition where the cause of action and relief remain unchanged.
material_facts: The eldest member of the undivided Hindu joint family gave notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure as its karta.
The family partitioned after notice was given but before the suit was filed, and the divided members joined as plaintiffs.
The notice set out the joint family's cause of action and the relief later claimed in the suit.
The suit was brought against the State, and the cause of action and relief in the suit did not differ from those in the notice.
issues.conclusion: The notice was sufficient to sustain the suit brought by all the divided coparceners; a second notice was not required merely because the family partitioned before filing suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure is imperative and its requirements must be complied with, but a notice is to be reasonably construed rather than scrutinised artificially or pedantically. The court considers whether the notice identifies the plaintiff, states the cause of action and relief with sufficient particularity, is delivered to the proper authority, and allows the required interval before suit. The object is to give the Government or public servant an opportunity to reconsider its position and settle or remedy the claim. Under Dhian Singh Sobha Singh v. Union of India, strict compliance does not require a pedantic reading; State of Andhra Pradesh v. Gundugola Venkata Suryanarayan Garu supports treating a notice and suit as sufficiently aligned despite a difference in the persons who gave notice and filed suit where the grievance and relief are representative. Vellayan Chettiar v. Government of the Province of Madras and Government of the Province of Bombay v. Pestonji Ardeshir Wadia were distinguished because their material facts differed.

rule.if: suit_against_government_requiring_pre_suit_notice and karta_gave_notice_for_joint_family and family_partitioned_after_notice_before_suit and divided_coparceners_brought_suit and cause_and_relief_unchanged

predicates.suit_against_government_requiring_pre_su: The proceeding is a suit against the Government for which notice must be given before suit.
predicates.karta_gave_notice_for_joint_family: The karta gave notice in a representative capacity on behalf of the joint family.
predicates.family_partitioned_after_notice_before_s: The joint family partitioned after notice was given and before the suit was filed.
predicates.divided_coparceners_brought_suit: The coparceners who became divided members brought the suit together.
predicates.cause_and_relief_unchanged: The cause of action and relief stated in the notice remained the same in the suit.

issues.definition: When a karta gives notice for a joint family, the family partitions before suit, the divided coparceners bring the suit, and the cause and relief remain unchanged, the notice is effective for them.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant does not establish a title based on long possession when reliable evidence fails to prove possession over the relevant historical period and the land was consistently recognised as Government property.
material_facts: The plaintiffs claimed that they and their ancestors had possessed the disputed land and had acquired the status of Raiyat Sarkar.
Older settlement records identified the Government as owner; later records did not reliably record the plaintiffs' possession, and the land was again recorded as Government property.
The plaintiffs produced no reliable oral or documentary evidence of their or their ancestors' possession for the period from 1891 to 1932.
A settlement proclamation invited objections concerning vacant sites, but no claim was made on the plaintiffs' behalf.
The evidence and receipts produced by the plaintiffs concerned later periods and were found unreliable or insufficient to establish the claimed historical possession.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs failed to establish their claimed title by long possession, and the State was justified in treating the land as Government property and setting aside the Deputy Commissioner's order in their favour.
issues.legal_principle: The claimant had to prove possession for the asserted statutory period through reliable evidence. Settlement entries recording Government ownership, the absence of reliable evidence of possession during the relevant period, and the failure to claim during the settlement proceedings defeated the claim. The Central Provinces Settlement Instructions passage relied on by the plaintiffs applied to land whose ownership was unknown, not to land recorded as Government property. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.suit_seeking_title_based_on_long_possess: The proceeding seeks recognition of a land title claimed to arise from long possession.
predicates.claimant_lacks_reliable_evidence_of_rele: The claimant does not provide reliable evidence that the claimant or predecessors possessed the land during the period needed to support the claim.
predicates.government_ownership_consistently_record: The land records consistently identify the Government as owner rather than recording the claimant's ownership or tenancy right.

issues.definition: In a suit claiming land title from long possession, the claimant fails to establish that title when reliable evidence of the relevant historical possession is lacking and the land records consistently identify the Government as owner.
